topics.label: Trade and wage inequality: the foundational debate
topics.summary: The 1990s–2000s literature asking whether trade or technology drove rising skill premia, which frames every later empirical design.

claims.title: The Impact of Outsourcing and High-Technology Capital on Wages: Estimates for the United States, 1979–1990
claims.rationale: Canonical industry-level decomposition of the skill premium into outsourcing versus technology; establishes that trade in intermediates can raise inequality even in a Heckscher-Ohlin world.

claims.title: Distributional Effects of Globalization in Developing Countries
claims.rationale: Standard survey of how liberalization affected wages, poverty and inequality in developing economies; explains why Stolper-Samuelson predictions failed and sets up the regional-exposure approach.

claims.title: Trade and Wages, Reconsidered
claims.rationale: Krugman revisits his 1990s view that trade effects on wages were small, arguing that trade with low-wage countries had become large enough to matter; a concise bridge from the old debate to the China-shock era.

topics.label: Shift-share (Bartik) identification
topics.summary: The econometrics behind regional exposure designs: what shift-share instruments identify and when they are valid.

claims.title: Bartik Instruments: What, When, Why, and How
claims.rationale: Shows the shift-share estimator is equivalent to using exposure shares as instruments, so identification rests on exogenous shares; includes diagnostics applied directly to the China-shock design.

claims.title: Quasi-Experimental Shift-Share Research Designs
claims.rationale: The complementary view: identification from as-good-as-random industry shocks rather than shares; re-examines Autor-Dorn-Hanson and gives valid inference for shock-level designs.

topics.label: The China shock and local labor markets
topics.summary: Regional and worker-level evidence on how import competition from China reshaped US and European employment, wages and transfers.

claims.title: The China Syndrome: Local Labor Market Effects of Import Competition in the United States
claims.rationale: The paper that launched the modern literature: commuting-zone exposure to Chinese imports, instrumented with other rich countries' imports, lowers manufacturing employment, wages and raises transfer receipt.

claims.title: Trade Adjustment: Worker-Level Evidence
claims.rationale: Moves from regions to individuals using Social Security earnings records; shows trade exposure lowers cumulative earnings and that low-wage workers bear the adjustment costs.

claims.title: The Surprisingly Swift Decline of US Manufacturing Employment
claims.rationale: Alternative identification using the 2001 grant of Permanent Normal Trade Relations to China; the removal of tariff uncertainty explains the post-2000 collapse in manufacturing jobs.

claims.title: The China Shock: Learning from Labor-Market Adjustment to Large Changes in Trade
claims.rationale: The authors' own synthesis of the China-shock literature across countries and outcomes, with an explicit discussion of why adjustment was slow and incomplete.

claims.title: On the Persistence of the China Shock
claims.rationale: Extends the analysis to 2019: exposed commuting zones never recovered, population did not adjust, and the shock's effects persisted long after Chinese import growth plateaued.

topics.label: Trade liberalization and regional outcomes in developing countries
topics.summary: Regional-exposure evidence from India and Brazil showing that tariff cuts have persistent, geographically concentrated distributional effects.

claims.title: Factor Immobility and Regional Impacts of Trade Liberalization: Evidence on Poverty from India
claims.rationale: Early regional-exposure design predating the China-shock papers: Indian districts more exposed to the 1991 tariff reform saw slower poverty reduction, with limited labor mobility as the mechanism.

claims.title: Trade Liberalization and Regional Dynamics
claims.rationale: Brazil's 1990s liberalization: regional effects on earnings grow for two decades rather than fading, driven by slow capital adjustment and agglomeration; a key benchmark for persistence.

topics.label: Structural and general-equilibrium models of trade adjustment
topics.summary: Dynamic and spatial models that quantify aggregate versus distributional effects and the costs of worker reallocation.

claims.title: Trade Shocks and Labor Adjustment: A Structural Empirical Approach
claims.rationale: Introduces the estimable dynamic discrete-choice model of sectoral mobility; finds large switching costs, which explains why trade shocks generate slow adjustment and sizable losses for incumbents.

claims.title: Trade and Labor Market Dynamics: General Equilibrium Analysis of the China Trade Shock
claims.rationale: Embeds the Artuç-Chaudhuri-McLaren mobility structure in a multi-region, multi-sector trade model; quantifies aggregate US gains from the China shock alongside concentrated regional losses.

topics.label: Political and social consequences of import competition
topics.summary: Downstream effects of trade exposure on voting, polarization, and social outcomes.

claims.title: Importing Political Polarization? The Electoral Consequences of Rising Trade Exposure
claims.rationale: Applies the China-shock design to US congressional and presidential elections; exposure shifts districts toward ideological extremes and contributed to the 2016 outcome.

claims.title: The Trade Origins of Economic Nationalism: Import Competition and Voting Behavior in Western Europe
claims.rationale: The European counterpart: regional Chinese import exposure predicts support for nationalist and radical-right parties across 15 countries, showing the political effect is not US-specific.

topics.label: Firm heterogeneity, offshoring and the consumption side of inequality
topics.summary: Within-industry wage dispersion driven by exporters, and the price-channel gains that offset wage effects for poorer households.

claims.title: Trade and Inequality: From Theory to Estimation
claims.rationale: Structural estimation on Brazilian linked employer-employee data of a model where exporters pay higher wages; most inequality growth is within sector-occupation, driven by firm heterogeneity.

claims.title: The Wage Effects of Offshoring: Evidence from Danish Matched Worker-Firm Data
claims.rationale: Matched data isolate offshoring from import competition: offshoring raises skilled wages and lowers unskilled wages within firms, with effects depending on task content.

claims.title: Measuring the Unequal Gains from Trade
claims.rationale: Shifts attention from earnings to expenditure: with non-homothetic preferences, trade lowers the relative price of goods the poor consume, so the consumption channel is pro-poor in most countries.
